That tokenizer had the SAME backtick/regex-literal corruption bug already found and fixed in geo-heatmap.js earlier this session: it mis-tokenized template-literal backticks and regex character classes containing quote characters, causing it to swallow large chunks of subsequent source into single bogus "label" strings (confirmed: 2 of the 83 entries were multi-KB blobs of concatenated code, not real labels), and it also miscounted the `function assert(cond, name, detail) {...}` DECLARATION line itself as an 83rd call site. The "83/83 match" was two runs of the same broken tool agreeing with itself, not real verification of file content.

cleanupOwnershipShortCircuitReview.claim: server-close and db-handle-close run UNCONDITIONALLY regardless of dbContext.ownsTempRoot; only the third step (dbContext-cleanup, i.e. temp DB file/root deletion) is gated on ownsTempRoot.
cleanupOwnershipShortCircuitReview.evidence: All three steps are passed as an array to the single dbHelper.runCleanupStepsAsync([...], primaryError) call -- NOT wrapped individually in handleOwnedCleanupAsync() (which would have gated ALL of them on ownsTempRoot). The ownsTempRoot check exists ONLY inside the third step's own fn() body: `fn: () => { if (dbContext && dbContext.ownsTempRoot) dbContext.cleanup(); } }`. Steps 1 and 2 have no such guard -- they always execute.

serverCloseStrategy.implementation: closeServerBounded(server, timeoutMs) helper function, called from the server-close cleanup step as `fn: () => closeServerBounded(server, SERVER_CLOSE_TIMEOUT_MS)` -- a direct return of the async call, not a fire-and-forget `() => { closeServerBounded(...); }` with no return.
steps: 1. server.close(cb) called -- synchronously stops accepting NEW connections (documented Node semantics), cb fires once existing connections end naturally.
2. Promise.race(closePromise, timeoutSignal) where timeoutSignal RESOLVES (not rejects) after timeoutMs -- avoids any unhandled-rejection risk from the timeout path itself.

3. If timeoutSignal wins: server.closeAllConnections() is called (Node core API, confirmed available via `typeof server.closeAllConnections === 'function'` on this Node v22.22.2 runtime -- not a hand-rolled Set-based socket tracker) to forcibly end any still-open connections.
4. The ORIGINAL closePromise (not a new one) is then genuinely awaited again, so the real close callback completion is observed, not assumed, even in the timeout path.
5. If closePromise wins normally (no timeout): clearTimeout(timeoutHandle) is called immediately so the pending timer cannot fire later and leak an event-loop tick after cleanup has already finished.
serverCloseStrategy.timeoutHandlingOnFire: server.closeAllConnections() (Node core), then re-await the original close promise -- not just reject-and-move-on
serverCloseStrategy.priorImplementationFlaw: The immediately-prior version used Promise.race([closePromise, timeoutRejectionPromise]) where the timeout branch REJECTED via an un-cleared setTimeout -- if closePromise won the race, that setTimeout was never cleared and would still fire uselessly later; if the timeout won, closePromise was abandoned entirely with no further waiting, meaning the server (and any of its sockets) could still be alive when the function returned. Both defects are fixed in the current implementation.

Fixed by moving clearTimeout() into a real finally covering the whole function body.

serverCloseStrategy.guaranteeStatementCorrected: The graceful-close grace period is bounded by SERVER_CLOSE_TIMEOUT_MS; after that, ordinary HTTP connections are force-closed and the original close completion is still awaited. This is NOT a claim that the entire close operation is guaranteed to finish within 5 seconds -- there is no second hard deadline on top of the force-close + re-await sequence.

dbHandleCloseSafety.methodExists: Confirmed by reading node_modules/sql.js/dist/sql-wasm.js directly: `e.prototype.close=function(){null!==this.db&&(...)}' -- the close() method exists on the underlying sql.js Database object exposed via db._db.
dbHandleCloseSafety.idempotent: Confirmed from the same source: the implementation guards on `null !== this.db` before doing any teardown work, and the guarded block sets internal state such that a second call is a safe no-op. Additionally, this file's own cleanup step sets `dbHandle = null` immediately after a successful close, as a second, script-level guard preventing any subsequent cleanup step from attempting to close or query the same handle again.
dbHandleCloseSafety.onlyClosesThisChildsOwnHandle: dbHandle is a module-scope variable local to this script, assigned only from this process's own `getDb()` call inside main() -- it never references a parent process's DB object (there is no cross-process handle sharing mechanism in this codebase).
dbHandleCloseSafety.parentProvidedMeansPathOwnershipNotHandl: A parent-provided POS_DB_PATH/POS_DB_TEMP_ROOT means the FILE and ROOT DIRECTORY belong to the parent (so this script must not delete them) -- it does NOT mean the in-process sql.js Database OBJECT this script itself created via getDb() belongs to the parent. That object is process-local either way and is always safe (and necessary) to close.
dbHandleCloseSafety.noQueryAfterClose: db-handle-close is the second-to-last step in the cleanup sequence (before only dbContext-cleanup, which never touches the DB object, only files/directories) -- no subsequent step queries the DB.

generationAndRetryStateMachine.reason: Two real boundary cases in the concurrent-close state machine were audited and fixed: (1) a server closed then re-listen()'d would previously hit the stale completed state and no-op, leaking the re-listened server; (2) a failed original close would previously be marked completed anyway, permanently blocking any retry.

generationAndRetryStateMachine.bugFoundDuringTestDesign: Initial versions of HTTPCLOSE11/12 had bugs in the TEST setup itself (double-wrapping server.close on re-listen; a mock that let the real close succeed while only faking an error report to the helper, which made a "failed" first attempt actually already-closed by the time of the second call). Both were caught by 2 real test failures (not silently passed), diagnosed, and fixed in the test code -- the underlying helper implementation was correct throughout; the tests needed fixing to correctly exercise it.
